title: One Month on Cash. The Envelope Experiment and What It Revealed
body: The rules were simple. One month, cash only for everything except bills and rent. Two hundred shekels per week in my pocket, in one envelope, and when the envelope was empty, the week was over. No borrowing from next week. Card stayed home except for emergencies, and I defined emergency in advance, in writing, because I know myself. Week one was a comedy. I had no idea what anything cost in cash terms. My card years had turned money into weather, something that happened to me. Standing at the register with actual notes produced a physical hesitation I had not felt since I was sixteen. The hesitation is the entire experiment. The card is a decision delayed. The note is a decision made, and I had gotten used to never quite deciding. Week two was the week of the small change problem. Coins multiplied in my pockets like a life form. I bought a small ceramic bowl for the door and learned why every grandmother has one. The bowl taught me a secondary lesson. Money you can see is money you can route. The loose coins funded two coffees and a bus ride that the card would have silently absorbed into a month-end number I would never meet. Week three broke me, as predicted. A work dinner, a friend's birthday gift, a pharmacy run, all in five days. The envelope was empty by Thursday. I sat with the written emergency definition and checked it honestly. The birthday did not qualify. I made the embarrassing call and moved four days of money from the next envelope, in front of a witness, meaning my partner, meaning the accounting was real. The old system would have hidden this. The envelope system made the overflow visible, and visible overflow is the only kind you can learn from. Week four was quiet and slightly holy. With one envelope and four days left, I planned meals around what was bought, walked past two shops I would have entered on autopilot, and found a twenty in last winter's coat, which felt less like luck than like a message from a previous, poorer version of myself. The numbers first, since they matter. I spent about eighteen percent less than my card month baseline, with the honest caveat that a watched month is a watched dieter. Some of that saving was performance. Some of it was real, and the real part has persisted, because I kept three habits. The envelope still feeds itself weekly. The ceramic bowl still routes the coins. The emergency definition still hangs inside a cabinet door. What the month actually revealed was not about money. It was about friction. My card life had removed friction from spending, and I had assumed friction was the enemy. It is not. Friction is the parking brake. The right amount of it stops drift without stopping the car. Cash restored exactly the right amount. Enough to feel. Not enough to matter. The card is back in my life for bills, online orders, and the rare emergency, which since the experiment has occurred zero times, though a plumber came close. The envelope sits by the door with next week's name on it in my handwriting. My grandmother used an envelope system her whole life, not as an experiment but as a given. I needed a month and a data set to arrive where she started. That, more than the savings, is what I took from the month.
